- If sentiment drops to 0.00 or negative in recent days, model should not assume continuation of upward trend; instead, expect sharp correction or mean reversion.
- When model forecasts show steady upward drift (e.g., +0.10–0.20/day) but true outcome shows sharp drop or volatility, reduce forecast slope or introduce early mean-reversion bias.
- If sentiment history shows recent negative sentiment (e.g., -0.14, 0.00) and model continues rising, apply downward bias correction, especially if forecast is >10% above recent high.
- If model forecast is flat or slightly rising but true outcome shows strong reversal (e.g., 30d drop from 90 to 75), assume sentiment-driven mean reversion and adjust forecast downward by 5–15% of current value.
- If sentiment history shows strong positive sentiment (e.g., 0.82–0.88) but model forecast is flat or slightly rising, consider that sentiment may be overestimated — reduce forecast slope or add early correction.
- If model forecast is rising sharply after a recent spike (e.g., 89.5 → 90.1 → 90.5) but true outcome shows a sharp drop or plateau, apply “overshoot correction” — reduce forecast by 2–5% per day after spike.
- If sentiment history shows no clear trend (e.g., 0.00 for 3+ days) and model continues rising, assume lack of momentum — reduce forecast slope or introduce volatility buffer.
- If true outcome shows strong upward movement after model forecast is flat or slightly rising, consider sentiment-driven momentum — increase forecast slope by 0.05–0.10 per day if sentiment >0.70.
- If model forecast is consistently above true outcome by 5–10% for 3+ days, apply “mean reversion bias” — reduce forecast by 1–3% per day if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- If sentiment history shows strong positive sentiment but true outcome is volatile or downward, assume sentiment is overestimated — reduce forecast slope or add volatility buffer.
